rayTEM thick-lens focal geometry

The three focal quantities of a thick lens, where each is referenced, and an interactive ray geometry for exploring them.

focal_powerEquivalent power, P = −C; used by aberrations.
focal_lengthEffective focal length, EFL = 1/P.
back_focal_distanceSigned exit-face-to-BFP distance, −A/C.

The three focal properties

A thick lens yields two valid focal quantities from the same traced ray, using ray heights referenced to different planes. rayTEM carries both, with the reference planes explicit in the naming.

The API:

NameDefinitionRole
focal_powerP = −CEntrance-height-to-exit-angle conversion; aberration pupil scale.
focal_lengthEFL = −1/C = 1/PConventional effective focal length, referenced to the rear principal plane.
back_focal_distanceBFD = −A/C = A/PSigned distance from the exit face to the output-space back focal plane.
There is deliberately no “BFD power”. The reciprocal of BFD is a valid exit-height-to-angle ratio, but it is not the equivalent optical power and must never be used as the pupil scale.

Two readings of one matrix

For one transverse axis in the Larmor frame, the full thick-lens body is represented by one entrance-to-exit matrix:

M=[ cos(KL)sin(KL)K −Ksin(KL)cos(KL) ] (1)

A parallel ray entering at height h exits with height Ah and slope Ch:

xexit=Ah,xexit′=Ch (2)
Entrance reference

Equivalent power and EFL

Divide the converging exit angle by the entrance height:

P=−C=Ksin(KL),EFL=1P (3)

This is the angle scale needed by the Krivanek aberration expressions.

Exit reference

Back focal distance

Divide the same exit angle by the exit height:

1BFD=−CA=Ktan(KL) (4)

This gives the drift geometry from the exit state to the BFP.

The sine-versus-tangent difference is therefore the factor A = cos(KL) introduced by using the smaller exit height. Both ratios are valid; the trap is using 1/BFD as though it were the equivalent focal power — through the aberration kick’s P⁴ dependence, that misscales every thick-lens aberration.

Interactive ray geometry

Use the ray-family buttons to switch between the back focal plane and a finite-conjugate image plane. Move either slider to see how the cardinal planes and physical rays evolve on opposite sides of KL = π/2. Lengths in the figure are normalized by 1/K.

Ray family

KL < π/2

KL > π/2

physical ray backward drift extrapolation finite-conjugate image actual internal crossover
Back focal plane
Rays sharing one incident angle meet at one point. Different incident angles map to different positions across the angular or diffraction plane.
Image plane
Rays leaving one finite object point at different angles reunite at one image point. Its location depends on the object conjugate.

The corresponding matrix conditions are:

Atotal=0at a BFP,Btotal=0at an image plane (5)

For representative rayTEM objectives, KL = 0.16 and approximately 1.3, so the left-hand case applies: EFL and BFD reach the same real downstream BFP from two different origins. The right-hand case is a useful edge condition. Once KL exceeds π/2, the physical parallel bundle has already crossed inside the field, while −A/C describes a virtual output-space BFP obtained by backward drift extrapolation of the exit rays.

Meaning of L and the lens center

In these expressions, L is the propagation length through the lens body, and the full matrix maps the entrance face to the exit face. Saying “L = 0 at the entrance” is shorthand for saying that the accumulated transfer begins there:

M(0)=I,M(L)=Mentrance→exit (6)

The magnetic field can be spatially symmetric about the center without making that center a crossover. For a parallel ray evaluated with the existing partial-length variable dz,

x(dz)=hcos(Kdz),dzcross=π2K (7)

The first crossover lies at the center only in the special case KL = π. Larmor rotation accumulates through the field, but the field center is not inherently a focal, image, or crossover plane.
